query: What algorithmic approaches have been proposed to maximize modularity for community detection, and what computational complexity does each report?
facets: identify the main modularity-maximization algorithm families (divisive, greedy, spectral)
attach each algorithm to its reported time complexity
state the largest network size each is claimed to handle

key_claims.text: the Girvan-Newman edge-betweenness algorithm runs in O(m^2 n) time, limiting it to small networks
Newman's spectral reformulation assigns nodes by the sign of the leading eigenvector of the modularity matrix B, running in O(n^2 log n) on sparse graphs
the Blondel et al. local-moving method runs in O(m) time and scales to networks with up to 10^9 edges

notes: Thesis 3.5. All three claims verified in thesis text. Multi-hop: algorithm -> complexity -> scale.

query: How is the modularity objective converted into a form solvable on quantum hardware, and what does each step of that conversion cost?
facets: explain why the delta(Ci,Cj) term blocks direct QUBO encoding
describe the one-hot / logical super-node construction that resolves it
state what penalty term the constraint requires and how its strength is chosen

key_claims.text: the standard modularity expression contains delta(Ci,Cj), which is not a quadratic binary function and therefore cannot be encoded directly onto the D-Wave system
a logical super-node of k binary variables per graph node, with the constraint that exactly one is active, converts k-community modularity maximization into a QUBO
the one-hot constraint is enforced by a penalty term with relaxation coefficient gamma, which is graph-dependent and has no known direct derivation from the modularity matrix B

notes: Thesis 4.4 and 4.7. The gamma-tuning claim is an explicitly acknowledged limitation, not an inference.

query: What encoding schemes are used to represent categorical variables in quantum combinatorial optimization, and what qubit cost and error tolerance does each carry?
facets: identify one-hot, binary, and error-correcting-code encodings
give the qubit count per node for each as a function of the number of categories K
state the minimum Hamming distance of each and what that implies for error correction

key_claims.text: one-hot encoding requires N x K qubits and any two distinct one-hot vectors are at Hamming distance 2
minimum distance 2 gives single error detection while minimum distance 3 is required for single error correction, so a distance-2 one-hot code can detect a single error but cannot correct it
Hamming(7,4) is a (7,4,3) code correcting one error; Hamming(8,4) adds a global parity bit giving d=4 and SECDED capability

notes: Thesis 2.6, 2.7. Three encodings x three attributes is a join, not a lookup -- the typed graph should win here. Coding-theory claims re-grounded on Hamming 1950 [22] (thesis cites Pless [37], a textbook not in the corpus). Verified against the Hamming PDF: Table V gives the distance-to-capability mapping; the closed form t=floor((d-1)/2) is NOT in Hamming and was reworded out.

query: Which mixer Hamiltonians have been proposed for QAOA on constrained problems, and what subspace does each preserve?
facets: identify the transverse-field mixer and the XY mixer
state which constraint subspace each preserves, if any
state the gate-count consequence of the choice

key_claims.text: the standard QAOA mixer is a transverse field sum of Pauli-X operators and does not preserve any constraint subspace
the XY mixer preserves Hamming weight within each qubit block, keeping the state inside the valid one-hot manifold throughout the circuit

notes: Thesis 5.3.1 and 7.5. Thesis states no codeword-preserving mixer exists for Hamming codes -- see open-t01.

query: Does quantum annealing actually outperform classical algorithms on modularity maximization, or does it only match them?
facets: state the modularity value the quantum annealer achieved on Zachary's Karate Club
compare it against the best classical value for the same graph
characterize what the claimed advantage actually consists of, if not a higher objective value

key_claims.text: the quantum annealer attained Q = 0.41979 on the Zachary Karate Club graph
that value matches, rather than exceeds, the record already obtained by the classical Blondel et al. algorithm

known_refutations.a: paper:19e9eaa00a36ed3334ea0c18b337a18d18f95c3e claims quantum annealing yields highly optimized community structures obtained all at once via the k-concurrent method, avoiding classical iterative heuristics
known_refutations.b: paper:19e9eaa00a36ed3334ea0c18b337a18d18f95c3e also reports the same QUBO solved on a classical annealer works for small graphs, and that larger graphs require the hybrid qbsolv decomposition whose mixing of classical and quantum processing degrades performance

notes: Genuine tension INSIDE one paper -- the headline claim vs the limitations section. Both sides verified in thesis 4.6/4.7. Tests whether the system surfaces a paper's own caveats.

query: Is modularity a reliable objective for community detection, or does it systematically fail on certain community structures?
facets: present the case for modularity as the dominant quality metric
present the resolution-limit evidence against it
state the conditions under which the failure occurs

key_claims.text: modularity compares intra-community edge density against a degree-preserving random null model, with real networks typically scoring Q in [0.3, 0.7]
modularity maximization exhibits a resolution limit: small communities are merged into larger ones when the optimal partition also contains large communities

known_refutations.a: paper:08b39cbabc2c5b764a85a0193296f83e23a62934 establishes modularity Q as the standard objective for judging partition quality, with positive Q indicating structure stronger than random
known_refutations.b: paper:39433dcfe25535df4398742432f2fb11330b0097 shows modularity maximization cannot resolve communities below a size threshold, so the optimal-Q partition can be structurally wrong

notes: The canonical disagreement in this literature. Thesis 3.4 and 4.2. Ring-of-cliques is the standard demonstration graph.

query: Do degeneracy and local optima in modularity maximization reflect a limitation of classical heuristics, or a property of the objective itself?
facets: state the degenerate-minima problem
present the position that it is an optimizer limitation motivating quantum methods
present the position that it is intrinsic to the modularity landscape

key_claims.text: modularity maximization admits multiple distinct partitions sharing the same modularity value, hindering convergence to a global optimum

known_refutations.a: paper:19e9eaa00a36ed3334ea0c18b337a18d18f95c3e frames degenerate minima as a limitation of classical heuristics that quantum annealing's concurrent search can bypass
known_refutations.b: paper:9be428c9383d47b86570b1b9fc20faf006346c5d treats the degeneracy as a property of the modularity function itself, which no change of solver removes

notes: VERIFY the b-side against Fortunato before committing -- the thesis attributes the framing but I have not confirmed the exact wording in the source.

query: What remains unsolved in designing constraint-preserving mixers for QAOA encodings?
facets: state which encodings currently have a constraint-preserving mixer
state which do not
distinguish open-because-nobody-tried from open-because-attempts-failed

key_claims.text: the XY mixer provides a constraint-preserving mixer for one-hot encoding by conserving Hamming weight per block

notes: Thesis 7.5 states no mixer restricting the state to valid Hamming codewords exists in the literature. This is open-because-nobody -- a good discriminator for the open-directions type.

query: What quantum hardware did the D-Wave community detection study use, and how many variables could each machine hold?
facets: name the D-Wave systems used
give the logical variable capacity of each
give the physical qubit count of each

key_claims.text: the study used the D-Wave 2X supporting 46 variables and the D-Wave 2000Q supporting 64 variables, with physical qubit capacities of 1152 and 2048 respectively

notes: Thesis 4.7. Single-source factual lookup -- vector retrieval should tie the graph here. Ties on lookup plus wins on relational is the honest thesis.

query: What time complexity does the Kernighan-Lin graph partitioning heuristic report, and what does its cumulative-gain step achieve?
facets: give the reported time complexity
explain what maximizing the cumulative partial sum of gains accomplishes

key_claims.text: the Kernighan-Lin procedure finds locally optimal partitions in time growing no faster than O(n^2 log n)
choosing the cut-point k that maximizes the cumulative gain sum lets the algorithm accept individually cost-increasing swaps, enabling escape from local optima

notes: Thesis 3.2.1. Replaces an earlier Pless-based numeric lookup that was unanswerable -- Pless is a textbook and is not in the corpus. Single-source lookup; vector retrieval should tie the graph here.
